# Incident Report — MTA 2024-08-15 PCAP Forensic Analysis

## 1. Scope of Evidence
Single artifact reviewed: `2024-08-15-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (18,189 frames, 11.7 MB, capture duration 1962 seconds / ~32.7 min). No separate IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence directory. All findings below are derived directly from packet content via `tshark`.

## 2. Victim / Infected Host
| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.8.15.133** | DHCP lease, ARP, NBNS |
| MAC address | **00:1c:bf:03:54:82** (Intel NIC) | DHCP Discover/Request, ARP |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-H8ALZBV** | DHCP option 12, NBNS name registrations, mDNS/LLMNR |
| AD domain | LAFONTAINEBLEU.ORG (NetBIOS: LAFONTAINEBLEU) | Kerberos realm, SRV DNS lookups, NBNS |
| Logged-in Windows user | **plucero** | Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString (`plucero`) issued from 10.8.15.133 to DC 10.8.15.4 |
| Domain Controller | 10.8.15.4 (WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS.lafontainebleu.org) | DHCP server, LDAP/Kerberos/CLDAP traffic |

## 3. Infection Chain (chronological)
1. **t=74.7s** — 10.8.15.133 (Edge/Chrome UA) sends `GET /managements?...` to **quote.checkfedexexp.com** (104.21.55.70 / 172.67.170.159, Cloudflare-fronted). Response: HTTP 200, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, a ZIP archive.
   - ZIP SHA256: `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5`
   - Contains a single file: **`Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js`** (fake-invoice lure), 6.99 MB, heavily padded with junk text/library code (evasion technique to inflate size past sandbox limits).
   - JS SHA256: `dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c`
   - t=100.3s: TLS session with SNI **business.checkfedexexp.com** (172.67.170.159) — same phishing infrastructure.

2. **t=135.9s** — Host issues a Windows BITS job (`User-Agent: Microsoft BITS/7.8`, HEAD then GET) directly to **`http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4`** — a bare IPv4 literal with **no preceding DNS lookup**. Retrieves a **PE32+ DLL** payload.
   - DLL SHA256: **`b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6`**
   - Embedded PDB path: `E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb`
   - Internal original filename: `release.dll`
   - (The other two BITS transfers seen around this time, to `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` / 199.232.210.172, are legitimate Windows Delivery Optimization traffic and unrelated to the intrusion.)

3. **t=196.9s → end of capture (t=1962s)** — Persistent C2 beaconing: **308 HTTP requests** (GET followed by POST, cyclic) from 10.8.15.133 to **72.5.43.29:80**, using a static, outdated spoofed User-Agent (`Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)`) with an encrypted/base64-like blob carried in the HTTP `Cookie` header (GET) and in the raw POST body. No cleartext tasking/data is visible; the DC-crypted channel is consistent with an active loader/backdoor implant polling for commands. Beaconing was still ongoing when the capture ended.

## 4. Malware Family
No externally-sourced threat intel was consulted (per instructions — no internet use). The only in-traffic identifier recovered is the implant's own build metadata:

- **Self-identified project name: "knock" (build `knock_v1.1.8`)**, per the PDB path embedded in the delivered DLL (`b7aec5f7...`).
- Attribution to this string is therefore **signature-level** (it is a literal artifact inside the malware binary), but I cannot map "knock" to a publicly-named commodity family without an external lookup, which is out of scope here.
- Beyond that string, everything else about the family (packed/stripped binary — only 345 printable strings recovered from the DLL; encrypted HTTP C2 with fake legacy browser UA; raw-IP C2 host with no DNS; JS-in-ZIP delivery abusing Windows BITS to sideload the payload) is **behavioral evidence** consistent with a loader/backdoor, not a confirmed public family name.

## 5. Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint**
- `72.5.43.29:80` (TCP) — persistent encrypted HTTP beacon/backdoor channel, no reverse DNS observed in traffic.

**Malicious domains**
- `quote.checkfedexexp.com` (104.21.55.70, 172.67.170.159) — phishing/malware delivery page
- `business.checkfedexexp.com` (172.67.170.159) — same actor's infrastructure, contacted via TLS

**Malicious URL**
- `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` — served the malicious ZIP
- `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — served the DLL implant

**Transferred files / hashes (SHA256)**
| File | SHA256 |
|---|---|
| Delivery ZIP (from checkfedexexp.com) | `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5` |
| `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js` (JS downloader inside ZIP) | `dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c` |
| `0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — PE32+ DLL implant ("knock" build, orig. filename `release.dll`) | `b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6` |

**Other artifacts**
- Fixed C2 beacon User-Agent: `Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)`
- Windows BITS (`Microsoft BITS/7.8`) abused as the delivery mechanism for the DLL implant (living-off-the-land technique, MITRE T1197)

## 6. Assessment
The host DESKTOP-H8ALZBV (10.8.15.133, user `plucero`) is compromised. The user visited a fake FedEx invoice site (checkfedexexp[.]com), downloaded a padded/obfuscated JScript downloader from a ZIP, which used a BITS job to fetch a DLL implant from a hardcoded IP (72.5.43.29) with no domain lookup. The implant then began continuous encrypted C2 beaconing to that same IP over port 80, active through the end of the capture. Recommend isolating the host, blocking `72.5.43.29` and the `checkfedexexp.com` domain family at the perimeter, and treating domain credentials for `plucero` as potentially compromised.
